hero.title: Zemun City Park
hero.subtitle: Belgrade's Century-Old Oasis Where East Meets West

intro.title: Discover Zemun City Park
intro.description:
When you cross the river from Belgrade's Old Town to Zemun, you'll instantly feel like you've stepped into another country — the architecture here is more reminiscent of Vienna or Budapest, and Zemun City Park is the perfect first stop to experience this lingering Austro-Hungarian charm.

As you enter the park, tall plane trees and ancient oaks form a green canopy overhead. Following the gentle stone paths deeper in, you'll be struck by a remarkable sense of harmony: an Orthodox church and a Catholic church stand side by side on the same lawn, as if silently recounting the days when people of different faiths prayed together in the former quarantine zone.

On nearby benches, students from Zemun High School review their lessons in the sunshine, while retired men focus intently on their chess games. There's no crowds or noise of the Old Town tourist spots here — every fallen leaf and every statue exudes an unhurried elegance. It's a living history museum and the gentlest green oasis in the daily life of Zemun's residents.

knowledge.title: The Charm of Zemun City Park

sections.title: A Century of Border History
sections.content: This was once the site of Europe's most famous border quarantine zone (Contumaz) from the late 18th to 19th century. At that time, Zemun belonged to the Austro-Hungarian Empire, while Belgrade across the river was under the Ottoman Turkish Empire. All merchants, travelers, and goods entering Europe from the East had to be quarantined here for weeks to prevent the spread of plague. In 1730, the Habsburg Monarchy established a strict border quarantine station here, serving as the first line of defense against plagues from the East. The quarantine station remained operational until 1872. In 1880, driven by local officials, this former 'quarantine zone of life and death' was transformed into a public green space with the first trees planted. Over the following decades, monasteries, schools, and women's colleges were built around the park, transforming it into Zemun's cultural and educational center. By the end of the 19th century, the quarantine zone had been completely transformed into a European classical-style city park, bearing witness to both the physical separation and cultural fusion of East and West.

sections.title: Architectural Features
sections.content: The park's most striking feature is two churches of different faiths standing side by side: the Orthodox Church of the Holy Archangel Gabriel (built 1786) and the Catholic Church of St. Roch (built 1836). Additionally, the magnificent Zemun First High School (Zemunska gimnazija) stands at the park's edge, along with nearly 2,000-year-old Roman sarcophagi. Both churches feature strong Baroque styling, while Zemun High School exhibits a splendid Neo-Renaissance character, together radiating the rich atmosphere of a Central European town.

sections.title: Cultural Significance
sections.content: Two churches belonging to Eastern and Western Christian traditions coexisting peacefully in the same park is a perfect microcosm of Zemun's — and Serbia's — religious tolerance and multicultural coexistence. As the 'back garden' of Zemun locals, it carries the childhood memories of generations and offers an authentic window into the peaceful daily life of Serbia. The park also preserves a monument to the French poet Lamartine and a memorial to the anti-fascist hostages executed in 1941, recording the heavy history of this land during World War II.

sections.title: Core Experience
sections.content: Stroll beneath the green canopy of century-old trees and feel the elegance and tranquility of a 19th-century European classical garden. Pause before the twin Baroque churches and appreciate the harmonious coexistence of Eastern and Western faiths on this land. In autumn, the century-old ginkgo tree showers the ground in golden leaves — a perfect setting for atmospheric portrait photography. On afternoon benches, watch Zemun High School students study in the sunshine while elderly men focus on their chess games — this is a living history museum and the gentlest green oasis in Zemun's daily life.

hours.title: Opening Hours
hours.tip: Recommended to visit in the morning or late afternoon, then stroll to the nearby Zemun Danube waterfront (Zemunski Kej)

tickets.title: Ticket Prices
tickets.tipContent: Zemun City Park is an open public green space with free admission 24/7. Both church exteriors are also free to visit. Church interior hours may be temporarily adjusted due to religious services.

transport.title: How to Get Here
transport.busDesc: From Belgrade's Old Town (near Republic Square or Studentski Trg), take bus lines 15, 84, 704, 706, or 707 across the Sava River. Get off at Zemun Pošta or Poljoprivredni fakultet station in Zemun, then walk 3-5 minutes to the park.
transport.walkDesc: If you're already in Zemun district, the park is within a 10-15 minute walk from the famous Zemun Market, Gardoš Tower, and the Danube waterfront.
transport.taxiDesc: A taxi from Belgrade city center to Zemun City Park takes about 15-20 minutes at an affordable price.
transport.tipsDesc: Zemun district has excellent public transportation. Buses are the most convenient option. If you're already in Zemun's Old Town, most attractions are within walking distance.

route.title: Recommended Route
route.overview: Recommended visit duration: 30-45 minutes. Perfect as the starting point for a 'Zemun Half-Day Tour.' After visiting the park, head east to the Danube waterfront or north to climb Gardoš Tower.
steps: Main Entrance & Roman Sarcophagi: Enter the park from Nemanjina Street and look for the ancient Roman sarcophagi displayed along the paths, feeling the deep historical roots of this land

Twin Churches Wonder: Walk to the park's core area to see the Orthodox Church of the Holy Archangel Gabriel and the Catholic Church of St. Roch standing side by side — compare their Baroque architectural details
Century-Old Ginkgo & Sculptures: Stroll along the shaded paths around the churches, find the monument to French poet Lamartine, and admire the golden foliage of the century-old ginkgo tree in autumn
Zemun High School Façade: Walk to the northern edge of the park to admire the magnificent Neo-Renaissance exterior of Zemun High School (built 1858), soaking in the academic atmosphere
Connect to the Danube Waterfront: Exit from the park's east side and walk a few blocks to the Zemun Danube promenade (Zemunski Kej) to feed swans or enjoy a riverside lunch
supplements: The park is fully flat and accessible for strollers and wheelchairs
Highly shaded by trees, making it a perfect summer retreat
Small children's playground facilities available, ideal for families with kids to take a short break

photoSpots.title: Photo Spots

spots.name: Twin Churches in One Frame
spots.desc: Stand on the central axis lawn in front of both churches and use a wide-angle lens to capture the Orthodox and Catholic churches together — incredible cultural tension

spots.name: Tree-Lined Avenue Depth
spots.desc: When morning sunlight pierces through the mist, stand in the center of the straight ancient tree path for a deeply layered European garden shot

spots.name: Zemun High School Vintage Façade
spots.desc: Use park foliage as foreground to capture the stately and ornate yellow building façade of Zemun High School

spots.name: Autumn Foliage Portraits
spots.desc: From late October to mid-November, the park lawns are carpeted with golden ginkgo leaves — the perfect setting for atmospheric autumn portraits

photoSpots.tipsContent: If you want to photograph inside the churches, please be quiet, avoid service times, and ask clergy for permission in advance (some Orthodox churches strictly prohibit interior photography). The golden ginkgo season in autumn is the best time for photography all year round.

hotels.title: Accommodation

hotels.name: Zemun Danube Botel (Waterfront Boat Hotel)
hotels.desc: Highly recommended — stay on a boat converted into a hotel moored on the Danube. Wake up, open the window, and feed the swans. Only a 10-minute walk to the park.

hotels.name: Zemun Old Town Boutique Guesthouses
hotels.desc: Choose Austro-Hungarian style boutique guesthouses near the market (Pijaca) or at the foot of Gardoš Tower for an authentic local lifestyle experience.

hotels.name: Zemun Modern Apartments
hotels.desc: Zemun offers many newly renovated modern apartments. Compared to Belgrade's Old Town, the same price gets you a larger, quieter space in Zemun.

hotels.supplementsContent: The biggest advantage of staying in Zemun is the peaceful atmosphere and excellent safety, offering an authentic small-town experience. While it's a bit farther from Belgrade's Old Town core attractions (like Kalemegdan Fortress), the excellent bus system (about 15 minutes) easily compensates for this.

items.name: Ming Z.
items.text: Absolutely stunning! The sight of two churches standing side by side blew me away — Orthodox and Catholic coexisting in the same park, the cultural atmosphere is so unique. The autumn ginkgo is simply breathtaking.

items.name: Hua L.
items.text: Very easy bus ride from Belgrade Old Town. The park is quiet and elegant, completely different from the hustle of the Old Town. That yellow Zemun High School building really feels like Vienna — every photo turns out amazing.

items.name: Fang W.
items.text: Strolling under century-old trees, watching elderly men play chess and students study — this is the most authentic Serbian daily life. Highly recommend combining with the Zemun Danube waterfront!

items.name: Wei C.
items.text: The park itself is free and very peaceful. The historical weight of the Roman sarcophagi is impressive. I recommend coming in the late afternoon — after the park, you can catch the sunset by the Danube. Note that church interiors are sometimes closed to visitors.

officialManagement.title: About Zemun City Park
officialManagement.text:
Zemun City Park is one of the most important urban green spaces and historic cultural landmarks in Belgrade's Zemun district.
It was once the site of Europe's most famous border quarantine zone (Contumaz) in the 18th century, witnessing the unique history of Eastern and Western empires converging here. After being transformed into a city park in 1880, it has served as an indispensable leisure space in the daily lives of Zemun residents for over a century. Today, the park is open to the public free of charge. The twin Baroque churches, ancient Roman sarcophagi, and the magnificent Zemun High School make it an excellent destination for experiencing Zemun's multicultural heritage and Central European small-town charm.
